The merged register contains 42 source-use records. Thirty-eight path/hash pairs passed checks; these contain 36 distinct held hashes. Repeated editions and source routes are retained. Seven newly acquired methods PDFs are in the local `methods/` directory; the western source work newly acquired Jansen 1989, Kenoyer's 2021-22 synthesis and Green and colleagues 2026. Eastern and documentary modules reused held sources. Download failures, including HTTP 403 and a publisher endpoint returning non-PDF content, remain in acquisition records. The successful alternate route for Singh 2017 is recorded separately from the failed one.

The register retains thirteen unknown phases with field-level reasons, conflicting locations, areas and chronology, a missing plate volume and preliminary/draft source status. Sixty readiness rows record five comparison prerequisites not assembled for each town. They are not assertions of archaeological absence. Six ratios of reported dimension pairs add a scoped arithmetic comparison with unspecified uncertainty; no new field measurements are added.

The module adds 118 source-qualified architectural, contextual and coverage assertions for Kalibangan, Banawali, Rakhigarhi, Surkotada, Kanmer, Shikarpur and Farmana. These records summarize ten previously acquired excavation-author/project reports. They do not add ten new publications, newly excavated structures, new radiocarbon determinations or new inscriptions. Earlier source observations remain separately identifiable in their original packages.

`sources.json` records each reused PDF's logical path, physical D: path, SHA-256, byte count, bibliographic identity, original URL, inspected pages and local-only handling. `observations.json` gives one assertion per record. `quantitative-table.json` selects the records with machine-readable values, units and their local denominator or scope. Values include excavation operations, building/room counts, outlined versus reconstructed areas, feature dimensions, rebuilding counts and source-specific dating claims. No missing field is replaced with zero.

The source audit preserves four conflicts: Kalibangan's original scan says 180 m for Period I east–west extent where the current Penn HTML says 160 m; Kanmer's printed interior area does not equal the product of its reported spans; Rakhigarhi's 300 ha statement does not match its 3 km-radius statement; Farmana's early chronology and later laboratory/editor discussion disagree. Farmana PLD-12422 also needs a sample/deposition join because the sample table uses a Harappan room label while its result table assigns a Gupta date.

They remain historical chronology, separate from calibrated BC. |

| Banawali | Open IA village; IB enclosure and repairs; IC rebuilt housing and bipartite/radial layout; Period II retains the inherited outline through further rebuilds | Later source estimates 8.8–9 ha town and 2.7–2.8 ha citadel; six identified citadel housing sectors; five streets converge at one gate; one excavated well at report date | About five centuries in Period II is the excavator's estimate. No construction-boundary model was recovered in the selected account. |

| Rakhigarhi | Early circular/rectangular structures and later lanes at RGR6; predecessor street arrangement retained in RGR2; fortification rebuilt between local phases IV and V | Draft reports seven mounds, but its 300 ha/3 km-radius statement is inconsistent; three RGR6 trenches; ten blocks in one L-shaped structure; seven rooms in a neighboring complex | Draft phase chronology is retained. Its BP ranges and inconsistent phase schemes do not provide a reliable duration for a named wall or town as a whole. |

| Surkotada | Early citadel/annexe enclosure; IA–IB retention with reinforcement and entrance changes; IC stone rebuilding and later passage blocking | Early house plans incomplete; IC inner citadel 60 × 60 m; nine listed rooms in one house group; 140 × 45 m southern excavation operation plus other trenches | Joshi's arithmetic BC dates and alternative endings are preserved. They have not been recalibrated or converted into a new occupation duration. |

| Kanmer | Pre-fortification I; massive IIa enclosure and aligned housing; IIb fills earlier open space while keeping orientation; III builds on or removes rampart masonry | Site 115 × 155 m and main mound 115 × 105 m are distinct definitions; one partly exposed 7 × 5 m space; eight partly exposed rooms in each of two later phases | Authors place most urban-phase AMS evidence around 2500–2000 BC. They leave beginning/end questions open and explicitly cannot explain older charcoal results. |

| Shikarpur | Mud-brick Phase I; increased use of local stone in II; patchy circular/apsidal structures and inferred stone reuse in III | About 3.4 ha mound; nine nominal 5 × 5 m trenches in 2007–08; southern wall base unreached | Relative phases only in this first-season architecture account; no occupation-boundary interval. |

| Farmana | Earlier pit dwelling/rectangular architecture; IIA–IIB broad plan retained; subsequent platforms, room additions and buttresses occupy lane/street space | Over 18 ha surface extent; intact central portion about 80 × 60 m; many partial complexes, including nine labelled rooms in Complex 4 | Shinde's early chronology conflicts with Osada's final synthesis and the report's AMS chapter. Laboratory intervals remain sample-specific. |

Kalibangan likewise defeats a single alignment label. The IAR 1967–68 account joins the earliest lower-city enclosure with the beginning of Harappan occupation, records nine corresponding building/road levels, and observes that houses nearer the perimeter follow the perimeter while those nearer the streets follow the streets. The source leaves the precise explanation open. Local adjustment and possible changes of street alignment are both discussed on printed p. 44. The broad lower-city plan therefore needs a geometric model with more than one reference line. Thapar's original scan describes four established N–S arterials and three E–W streets, with an indication of a fourth. The east–west lanes are staggered and do not cross every north–south arterial. A diagram of an ideal square grid would erase that distinction.

At Surkotada, the IA rampart was reused in IB with reinforcement; the residential entrance shifted, and the later IC rebuilding used substantial stone defences. Within IC, an intercommunicating passage was subsequently partly blocked. These observations permit a history of changing circulation without supposing that the whole settlement changed its orientation or government at each repair. The early and late lane widths in this module refer to different source contexts. They cannot be treated as a before/after narrowing of the same lane until a plan identity join is made. The main witnesses are [Joshi's report](https://archive.org/details/masi87excavationsatsurkotadaandkutchjagatpatijoshi_841_t), printed pp. 44–50 and 58, and *Indian Archaeology 1971–72*, pp. 13 and 16–17.

We read the entry, storage, data and writing instructions and the earlier town-axis and phase-link packages. We then used the previously acquired original reports, with web checks of their original author/institutional or archive access routes. The work selected architecture with explicit phase order, feature identities or exposure denominators. Re-reading held sources closed useful comparison fields without acquiring another large library.

Native PDF text worked for Farmana, Rakhigarhi, Kanmer, Shikarpur and the IAR reports. The Surkotada and Banawali volume scans required rendered page inspection. The Banawali folder contained the whole *Puratattva* 29 issue; we checked its title/copyright pages and located Bisht's paper before citing it. The Surkotada scan jumps from printed p. 41 to p. 44 at adjacent leaves, so the initial enclosure description uses the independently held IAR account. We preserved the limitation rather than reconstructing missing prose.

Visual comparison of Thapar's Kalibangan scan with the current publisher HTML found a 180 m/160 m transcription disagreement. The original scan controls the numeric register and the disagreement remains explicit. Arithmetic checks also revealed the printed Kanmer interior area and Rakhigarhi area/radius inconsistencies. These values remain source assertions with unresolved explanations, rather than revised measurements.

Farmana's report supplied the most useful local changes: bathing construction into a lane, a room occupying another lane, and a later buttress extending into street space. Its broad plan-retention statement can coexist with those named local alterations. The chronological chapters also disagree, and the AMS tables attach one Gupta determination to a label shared with a Harappan structure. We retained the individual claims to prevent an automatic site/room-name join from assigning an inscription or standing wall the wrong date.

The coordinator then supplied six enclosure-dimension ratios derived from the held source observations. We replaced the synthetic power chart with a native chart of those six architectural parts and retained the power gate in the prospective test sequence. The chart preserves the explicit Kalibangan source conflict in its notes and the lack of any dimension error model on the slide. The six ratios do not supply six independent towns or evidence for an intended canonical proportion.

Conceptual flow of the excavator's IA, IB, IC and II sequence. Housing clearance and a new bipartite/radial arrangement are assigned to IC, followed by rebuilding within the inherited outline. This is a sequence diagram, with no measured plan geometry.

Source-local examples preserve a bathing platform in East Area Lane 1, Structure 11A in East Area Lane 2 and an external strengthening wall at Structure 3I. Their broad IIA–IIB framework was retained. Schematics show the process, not actual plan geometry or a measured before/after width for one street.

Western and eastern agents own separate module directories; the inscriptions agent owns the documentary bridge. The coordinator owns methods, merged tables, figures, protocol, report, data update, retrospective and registry entry. We preserve other contributors' files. Integration reviews provenance, numbers and prose. The source-use record will distinguish new acquisitions, new uses of held sources and inherited observations.

We started from DATA.md, the registry, the town-axis and town-phase packages, current documentary work and the repository's research protocols. Three agents first owned distinct source modules: western towns, eastern towns and the inscription bridge. The coordinator owned the comparison, methods and proposed tests. Later assignments used separate review and visual-production paths. No agent edited another active contributor's files or the generated knowledge map.

Reviewed 24 October 2026. This review covers the versions read before the coordinator's prospective test-design file existed. The coordinator is adding a data-sufficiency gate and a synthetic sign-test power grid. No archaeological test is frozen or reported as passed. The methods already preserve the principal source distinctions: local phase names, incomplete excavation, different area definitions, uncertain entrances, household groupings and secondary deposits. The fourfold-orientation example is explicitly synthetic, and its value of 0.5 for two equal grids separated by 30 degrees is correct.

Add Rao directly to the card and define the extension as **phase-linked obligations for shared infrastructure, tested against domestic goods, ordinary ration distribution and workshop activities**. The current sentence “P1 alone moves credence to 0.18” is too permissive: a tablet association with provisioning could support ordinary ration or container records just as well. Require P3's independently coded distinction before any upward update of this specific claim. The coordinator has agreed to these two repairs.
